title: Unit 5c - Class Details Title Slide
summary: Title slide for CS103 Unit 5c on Class Details, covering advanced C++ class topics including constructors, destructors, initialization lists, and OO design principles.
main_text: This is the introductory title slide for Unit 5c of CS103, titled Class Details. The lecture is authored by Mark Redekopp. This unit covers advanced details of C++ classes including constructors, destructors, constructor initialization lists, object-oriented design ideals, headers and using statements, conditional compilation, default arguments, const keyword usage, nested types, and static members.
notes_text: This unit builds on prior knowledge of basic C++ class syntax and moves into deeper topics about how classes are constructed, destroyed, and organized in multi-file projects.

title: Reminders About C++ Classes
summary: Reviews key facts about C++ classes: access specifiers, operator limitations, the default assignment operator, and how classes can be used like any other data type.
main_text: Member data can be public or private (and later protected). Defaults is private, meaning only class functions can access private members. You must explicitly declare something public. Most common operators (e.g. ==, +, <<, >>, etc.) will NOT work by default with user-defined classes. You cannot cout an object directly (cout << myobject; will not work). The only operator you get for free is '=' which does a member-by-member (shallow) copy. Classes may be used just like any other data type (e.g. int). You can get pointers or references to them (Obj*, Obj&), pass them to functions (by copy, reference, or pointer), dynamically allocate them (new Obj, new Obj[100]), and return them from functions (Obj f1(int x);).
notes_text: Understanding that operators do not work by default on classes is critical for later topics on operator overloading. The shallow copy behavior of the default assignment operator can cause issues with dynamically allocated members.

title: Constructors Section Divider
summary: Section divider slide introducing the Constructors topic, which covers default and initializing constructors in C++ classes.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Constructors section of the lecture. The following slides will cover default constructors, initializing (overloaded) constructors, and the rules governing when the compiler provides a default constructor automatically.
notes_text: Constructors are one of the most important concepts in C++ class design as they control how objects are initialized when created.

title: C++ Classes: Default Constructors
summary: Explains default constructors (no arguments), their automatic generation by the compiler, and the difference between default and initializing constructors.
main_text: Constructors (aka ctors) are called when a class is instantiated allowing you to initialize data members to desired values. They have no return value. The Default (no argument) Constructor can have one or none in a class. Its signature is ClassName(). If a class defines NO constructors, C++ will create a default constructor for you, but it is just an empty constructor. For example: Student::Student() { }. Overloaded/Initializing Constructors are covered on the next slide. Code example shows a Student class with a default constructor Student() and an initializing constructor Student(const string& name), with private members string name_, int id_, and vector<int> grades_. A struct Item with no user-defined constructors gets a compiler-generated Item() constructor. When you declare Item x; it calls Item(). When you declare Item data[10]; it compiles because it calls Item() for all 10 items.
notes_text: The compiler only generates a default constructor if you define NO constructors at all. Once you define any constructor, you lose the free default constructor. This has implications for arrays and other scenarios that require default construction.

images.description: Code example showing Student class declaration with default and initializing constructors, and a struct Item demonstrating compiler-generated default constructor usage with arrays

title: C++ Classes: Initializing Constructors
summary: Covers overloaded/initializing constructors that take arguments, and the critical rule that defining any constructor removes the free default constructor.
main_text: Overloaded/Initializing Constructors can have zero or more. These constructors take in arguments. The appropriate version is called based on how many and what type of arguments are passed when a particular object is created. Examples: Student s1("Tristan"); and Student s2(123456789);. Important rule: If you define a constructor with arguments, the compiler will NOT give you the default constructor for free. When arrays of a type are declared, C++ automatically calls the default constructor for that type on each array element. That implies: no Default constructor means no arrays can be declared. So, you should also define a default constructor if you want to support arrays of that type. Code shows a Student class with the compiler-generated default constructor crossed out, two initializing constructors taking string and int respectively, and main() code that won't compile because Student x; and Student s[10]; require a default constructor.
notes_text: This is a common source of compiler errors for beginners. Always define a default constructor alongside initializing constructors if you need to create arrays or use the class in containers that require default construction.

images.description: Code example showing Student class with crossed-out compiler-generated default constructor and two initializing constructors, with main() demonstrating compilation failures

title: Examples of Constructors
summary: Shows four code examples comparing classes with no constructors, compiler-generated constructors, and user-defined initializing constructors, highlighting array declaration constraints.
main_text: Example 1a: Class Obj with no user-defined constructors has public setNum and getStr methods and private int num and string s1. Example 1b: The compiler generates a default constructor Obj() { } for this class. In main, Obj x; calls the default constructor. Example 2a: Class Obj with a user-defined initializing constructor Obj(int n, string s) { num = n; s1 = s; } and public members. Example 2b: When you define Obj() { } explicitly alongside Obj(int n, string s), the compiler does not generate a default constructor. In main(), Obj x, y[100]; will not compile if there is no default constructor. You can create objects with Obj y(5, "hi");. The key comparison: Case 1 gets a free default constructor allowing arrays and unparameterized declarations. Case 2 requires an explicit default constructor for arrays.
notes_text: The green arrows indicate code that compiles successfully, while red arrows indicate compilation failures. This side-by-side comparison makes the constructor generation rules concrete.

images.description: Four side-by-side code blocks labeled 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b showing class definitions with and without constructors, with green and red arrows indicating compilation success or failure

title: Identify that Constructor - Exercise
summary: Interactive exercise asking students to identify which constructors are called for Student and vector objects based on their declarations.
main_text: This exercise asks students to prototype what Student constructors are being called and whether they will compile. Given a Student class with a default constructor Student() and an initializing constructor Student(const string& name), with private members string name_, int id_, and vector<int> grades_. In main(): Student s1; calls which constructor? (blank for student to fill in). Student s2("Tommy", 12345); calls which constructor? (blank for student to fill in). Also asks to prototype what vector constructor is called: vector<int> vals(10); calls which vector constructor? (blank for student to fill in). The variable dat also has a blank for students to identify the constructor.
notes_text: This is a practice exercise to reinforce understanding of constructor resolution. Students should consider argument types and counts to determine which overloaded constructor is invoked.

images.description: Code showing Student class definition with constructors and main() with highlighted object declarations for students to analyze

title: Constructor Initialization Lists Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing constructor initialization lists for initializing data members of a class efficiently.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Constructor Initialization Lists section. Constructor initialization lists provide a mechanism for initializing data members of a class at construction time, which is especially important for members that are themselves objects. The following slides will explain why initialization lists are needed and how they differ from assignment in the constructor body.
notes_text: Initialization lists are a fundamental C++ concept that enables efficient one-step initialization of data members rather than the two-step default-construct-then-assign approach.

title: Consider this Struct/Class
summary: Introduces a Student struct with object-type members (string, vector) to motivate the need for constructor initialization lists.
main_text: Examine this struct/class definition of Student with members std::string name, int id, and std::vector<double> scores (say we want 10 test scores per student). The key question is: How can I initialize the members? The members themselves are objects (string and vector) and thus need their own constructors called. The struct has a default constructor Student() and an initializing constructor Student(std::string n, int ident). A potential initializing constructor implementation assigns name = n; id = ident; scores.resize(10); inside the constructor body. In main(), Student s1; calls the default constructor, and Student s2("Tommy", 12345); calls the initializing constructor.
notes_text: This slide sets up the problem: when data members are objects, simply assigning values in the constructor body is a two-step process (default construct, then reassign). The next slides explain why this matters and how initialization lists solve it.

images.description: Memory diagram showing Student struct layout with three fields: string name, int id, and scores vector

title: Composite Objects
summary: Explains that data member constructors are called BEFORE the object's constructor body executes, making it too late to call member constructors inside the body.
main_text: Fun Fact 4: Before the constructor of an object executes, all of its data members must be constructed. Analogy: Before a baby is born all its organs must develop and start working. Fun Fact 5: Constructors for objects get called (and can ONLY, EVER get called) at the time of creation (when memory is allocated). Once the object's constructor starts executing, it is too late to call data members' constructors. The data members have already been constructed. Code example shows a Student struct with std::string name, int id, and std::vector<double> scores. In the Student() default constructor, comments show that calling name("Tommy Trojan") and scores(10) are crossed out because they are TOO LATE TO CALL DATA MEMBER CONSTRUCTORS. Only id = 12313; works as simple assignment. In main(), Student s1; causes memory for Student to be allocated, and member constructors are called before the Student() body runs.
notes_text: This is the key insight that motivates initialization lists. By the time you enter the constructor body { }, all member objects have already been default-constructed. You cannot call their constructors again inside the body.

images.description: Memory diagram showing Student struct layout with name, id, and scores fields, alongside code with crossed-out constructor calls demonstrating what cannot be done
labels: TOO LATE TO CALL DATA MEMBER CONSTRUCTORS

title: Initializing Members - Construction Order
summary: Illustrates that when an object is constructed, constructors for each data member are implicitly called first, before the object's own constructor.
main_text: When an object is constructed, the constructor for each data member is implicitly called first. Member constructors are called BEFORE the object's constructor. A class Obj has three private members: Type1 mem1, Type2 mem2, Type3 mem3. The construction order is: (1) Type1() constructor for mem1 is called first, (2) Type2() constructor for mem2 is called second, (3) Type3() constructor for mem3 is called third, (4) Obj() constructor is called last. Members are constructed first, then the Obj constructor is called after.
notes_text: The order of member construction follows the order of declaration in the class, not the order in any initialization list. This is important to understand for debugging and for members that depend on each other.

images.description: Diagram showing nested ovals representing an Obj containing Type1, Type2, Type3 members, with numbered arrows showing construction order 1-2-3 for members then 4 for the object itself

title: Allocating and Deallocating Members
summary: Explains that construction works inside-out (smaller to larger) while destruction works outside-in (larger to smaller), showing the reverse ordering.
main_text: Members of an object have their constructor called automatically BEFORE the object's constructor executes. Construction works inside-out (from smaller to larger). When an object is destructed, the members are destructed automatically AFTER the object's destructor runs. Destruction works outside-in (from larger to smaller). Construction order: Type1() then Type2() then Type3() are called first, then ObjB() is called second. Destruction order: ~ObjB() destructor is called first to cleanup whatever members are referencing, then the destructor for each data member is called automatically: ~Type1(), ~Type2(), ~Type3().
notes_text: The reverse ordering of construction and destruction is analogous to stack behavior (LIFO). The object's destructor runs first so it can clean up any resources that reference its members before those members are destroyed.

images.description: Two diagrams showing construction (inside-out, members first then object) and destruction (outside-in, object destructor first then members) with numbered arrows

title: What NOT to do - Constructor Initialization Pitfalls
summary: Demonstrates that calling constructors on data members inside the constructor body creates local variables instead of initializing the actual members, showing a stack memory diagram.
main_text: We CANNOT call constructors on data members INSIDE the constructor. So, what can we do? Use initialization lists! Code example shows a Student struct with std::string name, int id, and std::vector<double> scores. In the Student() constructor body, writing string name("Tommy"); or name("Tommy") and vector<double> scores(10); would create local variables that immediately die at the end of the constructor. The actual object data members would be left uninitialized. A stack memory diagram shows two Student stack frames: the Student() constructor frame at addresses 0xbe0-0xbec and main's s1 frame at 0xbf0-0xbfc. The local variables in Student() are separate from the actual s1 data members, demonstrating that the actual object data members would be left uninitialized.
notes_text: This is a critical mistake to avoid. Writing Type member(args); inside a constructor body creates a new local variable, not a call to the member's constructor. The member has already been default-constructed before the body executes.

images.description: Stack memory diagram showing Student() and main stack frames with arrows indicating that local variables in the constructor are separate from the actual s1 object members

title: Old Initialization Approach - Two-Step Process
summary: Shows how assigning values in the constructor body is a two-step process: default construct first, then replace with desired value, which is inefficient.
main_text: If you write a constructor that assigns values in the body like Student::Student() { name = "Tommy Trojan"; id = 12313; scores.resize(10); }, the compiler will still generate the equivalent of Student::Student() : name(), id(), scores() which calls string(), int(), vector<double>() default constructors first. Then inside the body it modifies: name = "Tommy Trojan"; id = 12313; scores.resize(10);. Though you do not see it, realize that the default constructors are implicitly called for each data member before entering the { } of your constructor. You can then assign values (left side code). But this is a 2-step process: 1.) default construct, then 2.) replace with desired value.
notes_text: The two-step approach is wasteful because you first default-construct each member and then immediately overwrite with the desired value. Initialization lists eliminate this redundancy by constructing members with the correct values from the start.

images.description: Side-by-side code comparison showing user-written constructor on left and what the compiler actually generates on right, with an arrow between them
labels: The compiler will still generate this.

title: New Initialization Approach - Constructor Initialization Lists
summary: Introduces the one-step initialization approach using C++ constructor initialization lists to call member constructors directly at memory allocation time.
main_text: Instead of the two-step approach (default construct then reassign), we can initialize with a 1-step process using a C++ constructor initialization list. The syntax is: Constructor(arguments) : member1(param/val), member2(param/val), ..., memberN(param/val) { ... }. We are really calling the respective constructors for each data member at the time memory is allocated. Example comparison: The old way with Student::Student() : name(), id(), scores() (compiler generated) followed by body assignments gets replaced with Student::Student() : name("Tommy"), id(12313), scores(10) { } where you call the member constructors in the initialization list context. The left side shows default constructors implicitly called and then values reassigned in the constructor. The right side shows calling member constructors directly in the initialization list, which is the preferred one-step approach.
notes_text: Initialization lists are not just a style preference; for some types (like const members or reference members), they are the ONLY way to initialize. This is considered best practice in modern C++.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of old two-step initialization versus new one-step initialization list approach with arrow showing the transformation
labels: member constructors in the initialization list context

title: Summary - Initialization Lists vs Constructor Body
summary: Summarizes that values can be assigned in the constructor body but initialization lists are preferred, especially for non-primitive object members.
main_text: You can still assign data members in the { } body of the constructor. But any member not in the initialization list will have its default constructor invoked before the { }. You can still assign values in the constructor but realize that the default constructors will have been called already. So, if you know what value you want to assign a data member it's good practice to do it in the initialization list. Example: Student::Student() : name("Tommy"), id(12313), scores(10) { } - This would be the preferred approach especially for any non-primitive type members (i.e. an object). The left side shows assignment in the body: Student::Student() { name = "Tommy Trojan"; id = 12313; scores.resize(10); }. The right side shows the compiler-generated version with default constructors called first, then body assignments.
notes_text: For primitive types like int, the difference is negligible. But for complex objects like strings and vectors, using initialization lists avoids unnecessary default construction followed by reassignment.

images.description: Side-by-side code comparison showing constructor body assignment versus initialization list with compiler-generated default constructors
labels: You can still assign data members in the {...}
But any member not in the initialization list will have its default constructor invoked before the {...}

title: Calling Constructors - Common Mistake
summary: Warns against calling one constructor from another constructor within the same class, as it creates a temporary anonymous object instead of initializing the current object.
main_text: You CANNOT use one constructor as a helper function to help initialize members. DON'T call one constructor from another constructor for your class. Code example: A Student struct with std::string name, int id, std::vector<double> scores, a default constructor Student() : name("Tommy"), id(-1), scores(10) { }, and an initializing constructor Student(string n) that attempts to call Student(); inside its body followed by name = n;. The question is: Can we use Student() inside Student(string name) to initialize the data members to defaults and then just replace the name? No! Calling a constructor always allocates memory for another object. So rather than initializing the members of s1, we have created some new, anonymous Student object which will die at the end of the constructor. In main(), Student s1("Jane Doe"); would not behave as expected.
notes_text: C++11 introduced delegating constructors which do allow one constructor to call another, but this slide addresses the naive approach of calling a constructor inside the body, which creates a temporary object instead.

images.description: Code example with red arrows showing the incorrect approach of calling Student() inside Student(string n), alongside a memory layout diagram showing name, id, scores fields
labels: No!! Calling a constructor always allocates memory for another object

title: C++ Classes: Destructors
summary: Explains destructors: when they are called, their syntax (~ClassName), and when you need to write one to clean up dynamically allocated memory.
main_text: Destructors are called when an object goes out of scope or is freed from the heap (by delete). Destructors can have one or none (if no destructor defined by the programmer, compiler will generate an empty destructor). They have no return value and have the name ~ClassName(). Data members of an object have their destructor's called automatically upon completion of the destructor. Why use a destructor? Not necessary in simple cases. Use them to clean up resources that won't go away automatically, e.g. when data members are pointing to dynamically allocated memory that should be deallocated when the object goes out of scope. Destructors are only needed if there are external resources (beyond your immediate data members) that must be cleaned up or freed (e.g. release resources, close files, deallocate what pointers are pointing to, etc.). Code example: class Thing with string s1 and int* x. Thing::Thing() sets s1 = "Hi", allocates x = new int, and sets *x = 7. Thing::~Thing() calls delete x; to free the dynamically allocated memory, then data members are destructed after.
notes_text: The Rule of Three states that if you need a destructor, you likely also need a copy constructor and copy assignment operator. This will be covered in later units.

images.description: Memory diagram showing Thing object with s1 pointing to 'Hi' and x pointing to address 0x148 which holds value 7, alongside constructor and destructor code

title: C++ Classes: Other Notes - File Organization
summary: Explains how to split class code across header (.h) and implementation (.cpp) files, and why 'using namespace' should not be in header files.
main_text: Classes should be split across two files: class.h contains the interface description (class declaration), and class.cpp contains the implementation details (member function definitions). Example shows deck.h with #ifndef DECK_H, #define DECK_H, #include <vector>, the Deck class declaration with Deck() constructor and private std::vector<int> cards_ member, and #endif. The deck.cpp file includes "deck.h" and implements Deck::Deck() which fills cards_ with values 0-51 using push_back. Important: DON'T put 'using namespace' statements in header (.h) files. A bad example shows deck.h with 'using namespace std;' which forces anyone who includes the header to use that namespace. The correct approach is to either qualify types with std:: in headers, or only use 'using namespace std;' in .cpp files.
notes_text: Header guards (#ifndef/#define/#endif) prevent multiple inclusion errors. The separation of interface (.h) and implementation (.cpp) is a fundamental C++ practice that supports encapsulation and separate compilation.

images.description: Two pairs of code blocks showing correct and incorrect header file organization, with labels deck.h, deck.cpp, and app.cpp

title: Object Oriented Ideals Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the Object Oriented Ideals portion of the lecture covering encapsulation, abstraction, and design principles.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Object Oriented Ideals section. The following slides will cover OO design principles including encapsulation, abstraction, coupling, class design best practices, and the principle of placing computation where the data resides.
notes_text: Object-oriented design principles guide how classes should be structured to create maintainable, reusable, and robust software.

title: Before C++, There was C - Structs vs Classes
summary: Compares C structs (data only, all public) with C++ classes (data + functions, default private), showing the problem of unrestricted public access.
main_text: C introduced the idea of a struct, but it was different than it is now. In C: No class keyword, only struct. Structs ONLY allowed data members and everything was PUBLIC (any code could modify anything). There were some declaration nuances. In C++: Introduced classes (data + functions). Structs become equivalent to a class (data + member functions). Default access of struct is public whereas classes default to private. Code example shows a struct Deck with int cards[52] and int top_index. In main(), anyone can modify the members because they are public: d1.cards[0] = ACE; d1.top_index = 5; which is noted as probably not correct, demonstrating the danger of unrestricted public access.
notes_text: The evolution from C structs to C++ classes introduced the concept of access control, which is essential for data hiding and maintaining invariants. The public access of structs means any code can put the object into an invalid state.

images.description: Code showing a struct Deck with public members and main() demonstrating unrestricted access to cards and top_index

title: Class Notes - Data Member Persistence
summary: Demonstrates that data members persist across member function calls, allowing one function to modify data and another to access it.
main_text: Remember data members live on from one member function call to the next. They can be accessed within ANY member function. So, one member function might add to or set a data member, and another can use or access that data. Code example: class ABC with public void add_score(int s) and int get_score(int loc), and private vector<int> scores. The implementation of add_score calls scores.push_back(s), which would be seen by subsequent calls to member functions. The get_score function returns scores[loc]. In main(), ABC a; a.add_score(95); a.get_score(0); shows how data persists across calls.
notes_text: Data member persistence is what gives objects their state. Unlike local variables in functions, data members maintain their values between method calls, which is fundamental to how objects model real-world entities.

images.description: Code showing class ABC with add_score and get_score methods operating on a shared scores vector, demonstrating data persistence

title: Class Design - Naming and Object Discovery
summary: Provides guidelines for class design: class names should be nouns, method names should be verbs, and introduces object discovery and object invention.
main_text: Class names should be nouns. Method/Function names should be verbs. To decide what objects/classes you need, use two approaches: Object discovery means looking at the requirements description of the problem and identifying the nouns/objects. Object invention means creating objects that simplify management or help glue together the primary objects. Consider your previous projects to think of examples. Code example shows a GradeBook class with public computeAverage() and int* getScores() { return scores; } methods, private int scores[20] and int _size. The GradeBook::computeAverage() implementation sums scores and returns sum / _size. In main(), GradeBook gb; shows how the class might be used.
notes_text: Object discovery (finding nouns in requirements) and object invention (creating helper objects) are two complementary strategies for identifying the classes you need in a design.

images.description: Code showing GradeBook class with computeAverage and getScores methods, demonstrating class design with noun naming

title: Consider Previous Projects - Object Decomposition
summary: Shows how previous projects like TwentyOne and Connect4 can be decomposed into classes: Deck/Card/Player/Dealer and Board/HumanInputter/UserAIInputter.
main_text: Projects may vary based on semester. Two example project decompositions are shown. TwentyOne (Blackjack): Deck class containing multiple Card objects, Player class, and Dealer class. Connect4: Board class, Human Inputter class, and User AI Inputter class. Each project naturally decomposes into distinct objects with clear responsibilities, demonstrating how real programs use multiple interacting classes.
notes_text: Decomposing problems into classes is a skill that improves with practice. Each class should represent a single concept or entity with clear boundaries and responsibilities.

images.description: Two diagrams showing class decomposition: TwentyOne with Deck containing Cards alongside Player and Dealer; Connect4 with Board alongside Human Inputter and User AI Inputter

title: Good Design Principle 1 - Place Computation Where Data Resides
summary: States the OO design principle that computation should be placed in the object that owns the data, using member functions rather than exposing data externally.
main_text: Place the computation (code that operates on data) where the data is (i.e. in the object where the code resides). Use a member function to process the data vs. returning the data OUTSIDE for the 3rd party to process. See example on next slide. This principle means that instead of exposing internal data through getter functions and processing it externally, you should provide member functions that perform the computation internally and return only the result.
notes_text: This principle is central to encapsulation. By keeping computation with the data, you reduce coupling, make the code more maintainable, and prevent external code from depending on internal data representations.

title: Place Data and Code Together - Bad vs Good Example
summary: Contrasts a bad design (exposing internal array via getScores pointer) with a good design (providing computeAverage as a member function).
main_text: Place the computation where the data is. Bad approach (left): class GradeBook exposes data via int* getScores() { return scores; } which returns a pointer to the private scores array. In main(), external code retrieves the pointer and manually computes the average: int* myscores = gb.getScores(); then loops to sum. This exposes internal data and couples external code to the internal representation. Good approach (right): class GradeBook provides double computeAverage() as a member function. The implementation GradeBook::computeAverage() internally loops over scores[i] and returns sum / _size. In main(), the user simply calls double ans = gb.computeAverage(); which is cleaner and maintains encapsulation.
notes_text: The bad approach leaks the internal representation (a raw array) to external code. If the internal data structure changes (e.g., from array to vector), all external code that uses getScores() would break. The good approach shields callers from implementation details.

images.description: Side-by-side code comparison with prohibition symbol on bad approach (left, exposing scores via pointer) and star/checkmark on good approach (right, computing average internally)

title: Place Data and Code Together - Duplicate Slide
summary: Duplicate of slide 26 showing the same bad vs good design comparison for placing computation where data resides.
main_text: This slide is identical to slide 26 and reinforces the same concept. Place the computation where the data is. Bad approach exposes internal data via int* getScores() returning a pointer to the private scores array for external processing. Good approach provides double computeAverage() as a member function that processes data internally and returns only the result. The key takeaway is that member functions should encapsulate operations on data rather than exposing raw data to external code.
notes_text: This appears to be a duplicate slide, possibly included for emphasis or animation purposes in the original presentation.

images.description: Same side-by-side comparison as slide 26 showing bad approach with prohibition symbol and good approach with star

title: Classes and OO Ideals - Encapsulation, Abstraction, Composition
summary: Defines core OO concepts: encapsulation, abstraction, decomposition, composition, and delegation, with a Deck class example showing private data protection.
main_text: Classes are used as the primary way to organize code. The guiding motto is: Protect yourself from users and protect your users from themselves. Encapsulation: Place data and operations on data into one code unit. Protect who can access data via private members. Abstraction: Depend only on an interface (the what) regardless of implementation (the how) to create low degree of coupling between different components. Unit of decomposition that allows us to break our large software components into smaller, reusable components. Unit of composition that allows us to create larger and more powerful components from smaller ones. Delegation/separation of responsibility. Polymorphism and Inheritance (more on this later). Code example: class Deck with public Deck(), ~Deck(), shuffle(), cut(), get_top_card() and private int cards[52] and int top_index. In cardgame.cpp, d.shuffle() and d.cut() work, but d.cards[0] = ACE and d.top_index = 5 won't compile because they are private.
notes_text: These OO ideals are the foundation of good software design. Encapsulation protects invariants, abstraction enables modular design, and composition/decomposition manage complexity.

images.description: Deck class code example showing public interface methods and private data members, with cardgame.cpp demonstrating that private member access fails to compile

title: Coupling - Low vs Tight
summary: Defines coupling as dependency between components, compares low coupling (good, like replacing a car battery) with tight coupling (bad, like replacing a car engine).
main_text: Coupling refers to how much components depend on each other's implementation details (i.e. how much work it is to remove one component and drop in a new implementation of it). Low coupling (good) vs. Tight coupling (not so good). Analogies: Replacing a new battery in your car (low coupling, easy) vs. Replacing a new engine in your car (tight coupling, hard). Adding a USB device to your laptop (low coupling) vs. Replacing the CPU in your laptop (tight coupling). OO Design seeks to reduce coupling as much as possible by creating well-defined interfaces to update (write) or access (read) the state of an object, and allowing alternate implementations that do NOT require interface changes.
notes_text: Low coupling is achieved through well-defined interfaces. When components communicate only through interfaces, internal implementations can change without affecting other parts of the system.

title: Headers and Using Statements Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the topic of headers and using statements in C++ class organization.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Headers and Using Statements section. The following slides will cover how to properly use header files with namespaces, why using namespace statements should not appear in header files, and the correct way to qualify standard library types in headers versus source files.
notes_text: Proper header file management is essential for large C++ projects to avoid namespace pollution and compilation errors.

title: Headers and using Statements (1) - Two Options
summary: Shows that header files using vector and string need namespace resolution, comparing bad (using namespace std) and good (std:: qualification) approaches.
main_text: A deck.h header file with #include <vector> and #include <string> won't compile if vector and string are used without namespace qualification because they live in the 'std' namespace. Option 1 (BAD): Add 'using namespace std;' in .h files. This makes the header compile but forces the namespace on everyone who includes it. The Deck class can then use string and vector<int> without std:: prefix. Option 2 (GOOD): Qualify class names with 'std::' in .h files. The Deck class uses std::string for cardName() return type and std::vector<int> for the private cards member. This approach is clean and doesn't impose namespace choices on includers.
notes_text: Option 2 is the industry standard practice. Using std:: qualification in headers is more verbose but prevents namespace pollution and potential naming conflicts.

images.description: Three code blocks showing deck.h without namespace resolution (won't compile), Option 1 with using namespace std (BAD), and Option 2 with std:: qualification (GOOD)

title: Headers and using Statements (2) - Why Not in Headers
summary: Demonstrates that putting 'using' in headers causes namespace pollution, leading to name conflicts when includers define their own types with the same name.
main_text: By putting using statements in a header file, anyone who #includes your header is now automatically using that namespace. Rule: NEVER put a using statement in a header (.h) file. Example of the problem: deck.h with 'using namespace std;' and Deck class using string and vector<int>. In app.cpp, which #includes "deck.h", the comment notes 'GUESS I'M using namespace std; whether I like it or NOT!' If app.cpp defines its own class string { // My own implementation of 'string' }; and then declares string x; there is a compiler error because of a name conflict between the user's 'string' class and C++ std::string. The compiler cannot determine which string is used - the one from this file or std::string.
notes_text: This is a real-world problem in large codebases. Namespace pollution from headers can cause subtle and hard-to-debug compilation errors, especially when different libraries define types with common names.

images.description: Code showing deck.h with using namespace std and app.cpp demonstrating name conflict between user-defined string class and std::string

title: Headers and using Statements (3) - Using in .cpp Files
summary: Clarifies that it is fine and good to put 'using' statements in .cpp files since they are compiled separately and not included by other files.
main_text: Corollary: It is FINE AND GOOD to put using statements in .cpp files (since we don't #include .cpp files - they are each compiled separately). Example shows deck.h with std:: qualified types (Option 2: GOOD) and deck.cpp with #include "deck.h" followed by 'using namespace std;'. The deck.cpp implementation can then use string without the std:: prefix in function definitions like string Deck::cardName(). This works because .cpp files are compiled independently and their using statements do not leak into other translation units.
notes_text: The key distinction is that .h files are included into other files (and thus their using statements propagate), while .cpp files are compiled in isolation. Using statements in .cpp files only affect that single translation unit.

images.description: Code showing deck.h with std:: qualified types and deck.cpp with using namespace std, demonstrating the correct pattern

title: Summary - Header and Using Statement Rules
summary: Summarizes the rules: do NOT place using statements in headers, do precede types with std::; source files can freely use using statements.
main_text: Header (.h) files: Do NOT place using statements in header files. Do precede C++ class types with std:: (e.g., std::string, std::vector<int>). Source (.cpp) files: Feel free to add using statements as desired. If you do, then no need to precede type with std::. Code example shows deck.h using std::string and std::vector<int> (Option 2: GOOD). Below, app.cpp includes "deck.h" and defines its own class string without any naming conflict because the header does not inject std namespace. In main(), string x; clearly refers to the user-defined string class with no confusion.
notes_text: Following these rules consistently across a project prevents namespace-related compilation errors and makes headers safe to include from any context.

images.description: Summary code showing correct deck.h with std:: qualification and app.cpp with its own string class, demonstrating no conflict

title: Conditional Compilation Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing conditional compilation, covering header guards and preprocessor directives.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Conditional Compilation section. The following slides will cover header guards using #ifndef/#define/#endif, the problem of multiple inclusion, the #pragma once alternative, and using #ifdef for debug code.
notes_text: Conditional compilation is a preprocessor feature that controls which code gets compiled based on defined symbols, essential for both header guards and debug builds.

title: C++ Classes: Use Header Guards - The Problem
summary: Demonstrates how multiple headers including the same file leads to duplicate class definitions and compiler errors.
main_text: Many headers may include the same file. This may lead to multiple inclusions and definitions, causing compiler errors. Example: mystr.h defines class MyStr with a constructor MyStr() and private char* str_. student.h includes mystr.h and defines class Student with a MyStr name_ member. app.cpp includes both student.h and mystr.h. After preprocessing, app.cpp sees: class MyStr { ... }; (first definition from student.h's include), class Student { ... MyStr name_; };, then class MyStr { // second definition - error!! }; (from the direct include of mystr.h). The compiler sees two definitions of MyStr, which is an error.
notes_text: The One Definition Rule (ODR) in C++ states that each class can only be defined once in a translation unit. Without header guards, including the same header multiple times violates this rule.

images.description: Code showing mystr.h, student.h including mystr.h, and app.cpp including both, with an arrow showing the expanded result containing duplicate MyStr definitions

title: Conditional Compiler Directives / Header Guards
summary: Explains #define, #ifdef, #ifndef, and #endif preprocessor directives used to create header guards that prevent multiple inclusion.
main_text: Compiler directives start with '#'. #define XXX sets a flag named XXX in the compiler. #ifdef and #ifndef XXX ... #endif: Continue compiling code below until #endif, if XXX is (or is not) defined. To create header guards, nest header declarations inside: #ifndef XX, #define XX, ..., #endif. Newer versions of C++ (C++11 and beyond) support: #pragma once as an alternative. Example: mystr.h wrapped with #ifndef MYSTR_H, #define MYSTR_H, class MyStr { ... };, #endif. student.h includes mystr.h and defines Student. app.cpp includes student.h and mystr.h. The guards prevent the second inclusion of MyStr.
notes_text: The convention is to use uppercase filename with underscores as the guard symbol (e.g., MYSTR_H for mystr.h). This ensures uniqueness across different headers.

images.description: Code showing mystr.h with header guards, student.h including it, and app.cpp, demonstrating the #ifndef/#define/#endif pattern

title: C++ Classes: Use Header Guards - Solution
summary: Shows step-by-step how header guards work during preprocessing to prevent duplicate class definitions.
main_text: Header guards avoid multiple inclusion. Walkthrough of the preprocessing: app.cpp includes student.h which includes mystr.h. First encounter of mystr.h: #ifndef MYSTR_H - Compiler says: No, MYSTR_H hasn't been defined. So then it DEFINES it (e.g. set MYSTR_H = true) and includes class MyStr { ... };. Then class Student { ... MyStr name_; }; is included. Second encounter: app.cpp directly includes mystr.h again. #ifndef MYSTR_H - Compiler says: Yes, MYSTR_H has been defined, so do NOT include all the code and skip to #endif. The code header only got included once! This prevents the duplicate definition error.
notes_text: The header guard mechanism is simple but effective. The preprocessor tracks which symbols have been defined and conditionally includes or skips blocks of code accordingly.

images.description: Step-by-step diagram showing preprocessing flow: first inclusion defines MYSTR_H and includes the code, second inclusion skips because MYSTR_H is already defined

title: Alternative on Most C++ Compilers - #pragma once
summary: Introduces #pragma once as a simpler one-line alternative to the three-line #ifndef/#define/#endif header guard pattern.
main_text: Rather than 3 lines (#ifndef, #define, ..., #endif), use 1 line: #pragma once. Example comparison: The traditional header guard for mystr.h uses #ifndef MYSTR_H, #define MYSTR_H, class MyStr { public: MyStr(); private: char* str_; };, #endif. With #pragma once, the same file becomes simply: #pragma once, class MyStr { public: MyStr(); private: char* str_; };. The #pragma once directive tells the compiler to include this file only once per compilation, achieving the same effect with less boilerplate.
notes_text: #pragma once is supported by virtually all modern compilers (GCC, Clang, MSVC) but is not technically part of the C++ standard. It is generally preferred in practice for its simplicity.

images.description: Side-by-side comparison of traditional #ifndef/#define/#endif header guard versus the simpler #pragma once directive

title: Conditional Compilation for Debug Code
summary: Shows how #ifdef/#endif with -D compiler flags can conditionally include debug output code that is excluded from release builds.
main_text: Conditional compilation is often used to compile additional DEBUG code. Place code that is only needed for debugging and that you would not want to execute in a release version. Place code in a #ifdef NAME...#endif bracket. The compiler will only compile the code if a #define NAME is found. You can specify #define in the source code or at the compiler command line with the -DNAME flag: g++ -o stuff -DDEBUG stuff.cpp. Example: int main() with int x, sum=0, data[10]; A loop sums data[i]. Inside the loop, #ifdef DEBUG wraps cout << "Current sum is "; cout << sum << endl; #endif. After the loop, cout << "Total sum is "; is always compiled. By compiling with -DDEBUG, the debug output is included; without the flag, it is excluded.
notes_text: This technique is widely used in production code to include diagnostic output during development that can be stripped from release builds without changing source code.

images.description: Code example showing #ifdef DEBUG wrapping debug cout statements, with compiler command line showing -DDEBUG flag

title: Default Arguments Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing default arguments in C++ functions and constructors.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Default Arguments section. The following slides will cover how default arguments work, how they reduce the need for overloaded constructors, where to place default values (prototype vs definition), and limitations on default argument ordering.
notes_text: Default arguments are a C++ feature that can simplify class interfaces by reducing the number of overloaded functions needed.

title: Default Arguments - Motivation
summary: Motivates default arguments by showing how two similar constructors (default and initializing) for an IntVector class have redundant code.
main_text: Suppose we write our own vector class, IntVector, with two constructors: A Default constructor that defaults to an array of size 10, and an Initializing constructor that creates an array of size n provided by the user. Look at the similarity - doesn't it feel wasteful? Default arguments can help reduce the number of function overloads we need to write! The class IntVector has IntVector() (default constructor, suppose we default to size 10) and IntVector(size_t n) (initializing ctor creates array of size n), with private size_t n_ and int* array. The default constructor implementation: IntVector::IntVector() { n_ = 10; array = new int[10]; }. The initializing constructor: IntVector::IntVector(size_t n) { n_ = n; array = new int[n]; }. The two constructors are nearly identical, differing only in where the size value comes from.
notes_text: This pattern of having nearly identical constructors is very common and is exactly what default arguments are designed to eliminate.

images.description: Code showing IntVector class with two nearly identical constructors and their implementations

title: Default Arguments - Usage
summary: Shows how a single constructor with a default argument (size_t n = 10) replaces both the default and initializing constructors.
main_text: Default arguments do exactly what their name says: Provide a default value if the user does not provide one when they call the function. Now the same initializing ctor will be sufficient if the user provides an initial size or not (in which case it will use the default of 10). The IntVector class replaces both constructors with a single IntVector(size_t n = 10); The default constructor is crossed out because it is no longer needed. In main(): IntVector vec1(50); - user provides size 50, and IntVector vec2; - will use default of 10. Both call the same constructor above. Important: DO NOT REPEAT THE DEFAULT VALUE IN THE DEFINITION; ONLY IN THE PROTOTYPE. The definition is: IntVector::IntVector(size_t n) { n_ = n; array = new int[n_]; } without repeating the = 10.
notes_text: A key rule is that the default value appears only in the declaration (prototype), not in the definition. Repeating it in both places is a compiler error in most compilers.

images.description: Code showing IntVector class with a single constructor using default argument, crossed-out default constructor, and main() demonstrating both uses
labels: DO NOT REPEAT THE DEFAULT VALUE

title: Default Arguments - Prototype Only Rule
summary: Emphasizes that default argument values should only be listed in the prototype (declaration), not both the prototype and definition.
main_text: Only list the default argument in the prototype but not both the prototype and definition. The IntVector class shows the prototype with the default: IntVector(size_t n = 10); with a comment noting to usually put default arg in prototype. Private members are size_t n_ and int* array. The definition (implementation) uses an initialization list and does NOT repeat the default: IntVector::IntVector(size_t n) : n_(n) { array = new int[n_]; }. In main(): IntVector vec1(50); creates with size 50, and IntVector vec2; will use default 10. Both call the same constructor above.
notes_text: Putting the default value in the prototype ensures that callers can see the default from the declaration alone. The definition does not need to repeat it because the compiler already knows the default from the declaration.

images.description: Code showing IntVector with default argument in prototype only, and definition without the default, with main() usage examples

title: Other Limitations of Default Arguments
summary: Explains that default arguments must be at the END of the parameter list, and warns about ambiguity with overloaded functions.
main_text: You can have many default arguments, but they must be at the END of the argument list; a non-default argument CANNOT come AFTER a default argument. Ensure that two functions' signatures are not ambiguous. Good example: void good1(int a, int b = 10, string s = "hi"); - non-default first, defaults at end. Bad example (non-default after default): void bad1(int a, int b = 10, string s); - string s has no default but comes after b which does. Bad example (ambiguous overload): void good1(int b); alongside void good1(int a, int b = 10, string s = "hi"); - calling good1(5) is ambiguous. The compiler error shows: error: call of overloaded 'good1(int)' is ambiguous, with candidates void good1(int, int, std::string) and void good1(int).
notes_text: The ordering rule exists because the compiler fills in default values from right to left. If a non-default parameter were after a default one, the compiler could not determine which arguments were intentionally omitted.

images.description: Code examples showing good and bad default argument ordering, plus ambiguity error example with compiler error message
labels: error: call of overloaded 'good1(int)' is ambiguous

title: Review of Const Keyword Usage Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing a review of the const keyword and its three uses in member function prototypes.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Review of Const Keyword Usage section. The following slides will cover the three positions where const can appear in a member function prototype: with the return value, with input arguments, and at the end of the function to protect the calling object's data members.
notes_text: The const keyword is one of the most important tools for writing correct and safe C++ code. Understanding its three positions is essential for class design.

title: The const Keyword - Three Positions
summary: Identifies the three positions where const can appear in a member function prototype: return value, input arguments, and after the parameter list.
main_text: The const keyword can be used in 3 sections in a member function prototype: const int& MyArray::read(const string& a1, string& a2, const string& a3) const; The const in each section protects something different from being changed. Position 1: With the return value - ensures what is returned cannot be modified (usually when you return a reference/alias, what you are referencing cannot be changed). Position 2: Any or all input arguments - ensures that argument is NOT modified as the function runs. Position 3: At the end of the prototype of a member function - ensures THAT OBJECT's (the calling object's) data members are NOT modified by the function.
notes_text: Position 3 (const at the end) is unique to member functions and is part of the function signature. A const object can only call const member functions, making this declaration critical for const-correctness.

title: The const Keyword - Practical Example
summary: Demonstrates all three uses of const in a Roster class with getGrade function, showing how const protects arguments, data members, and return values.
main_text: The const keyword can be used with: 1. Input arguments to ensure they aren't modified. 2. After a member function to ensure data members of the calling object aren't modified. 3. Return values to ensure they aren't modified. Example: class Roster with private vector<string> names and vector<string> grades ("A+", "B-", etc.), and public const string& getGrade(const string& name) const; The function signature shows all three const positions. In usage: Roster rost; string n = "Jill"; const string& grade = rost.getGrade(n); grade = "A+"; // won't compile (const-ref). The diagram shows the getGrade stack with const string& name pointing to n, and main's stack with const string& grade pointing into the rost.grades vector, with lock icons representing const protection.
notes_text: The const reference return type prevents callers from modifying the internal data of the Roster through the returned reference. This is essential for maintaining encapsulation when returning references to internal data.

images.description: Stack diagram showing getGrade and main frames with arrows indicating const references pointing to Roster data members, with lock icons representing const protection

title: Exercises - Const Exercises
summary: Exercise slide prompting students to practice const keyword concepts covered in the lecture.
main_text: This slide contains a const exercises prompt for students to practice applying the const keyword in various positions of member function prototypes. Students should practice identifying where const should be placed and what each placement protects.
notes_text: Hands-on practice with const placement is essential for developing const-correctness habits in C++ programming.

title: Review Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing review exercises covering const arguments, const member functions, initialization lists, construction order, and friend functions.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Review section. The following slides contain review exercises on const function arguments, const member functions, constructor initialization lists, construction order, friend functions, and friend classes.
notes_text: These review exercises test comprehension of the major topics covered in this unit.

title: Review [1] - Const Arguments and Const Member Functions
summary: Review exercise with two problems: one on const function arguments (will code compile?) and one on const member functions (what does trailing const imply?).
main_text: Const function arguments exercise: Will this code compile? void f1(const vector<int>& x) { x.push_back(103); x.push_back(104); } - this modifies x which is const, so it won't compile. void f2(string& y) { y = "Bye"; } In main(): vector<int> a; string b = "Hi"; f1(a); f2(b); cout << b.size() << endl; - Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles). Const member functions exercise: What does the highlighted const keyword imply in the code below? class Item with int val, public void foo() and int bar() const. void Item::foo() { val = 5; } - modifies val. int Item::bar() const { return val+1; } - does not modify val. void f1(const Item& arg) { int x = arg.bar(); // fine. arg.foo(); // Compiler Error! } - const reference cannot call non-const member function.
notes_text: The f1 function won't compile because push_back modifies the vector, violating the const promise. The f2 function modifies b to "Bye" which has size 3. The const member function bar() cannot modify data members.

images.description: Two side-by-side code exercises: left showing const function argument problems, right showing const member function usage with Item class

title: Review [2] - Initialization Lists and Construction Order
summary: Review exercise on initialization lists (most efficient way to initialize members) and construction order (what gets printed when constructing composite objects).
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists exercise: What is the most efficient means to initialize the vals member to an initial array size of 20 and s to a user-defined string? class Thing with public Thing(const std::string& s_init), private vector<int> vals and string s. The constructor Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) currently has: // is this the most efficient way? vals.resize(20); s = s_init; in the body. Construction Order exercise: What is printed by the code below? class ABC with ABC() { cout << "ABC" << endl; }. class DEF with DEF() { cout << "DEF" << endl; }. class XYZ with ABC m1; DEF m2; and XYZ() { cout << "XYZ" << endl; }. int main() { XYZ x1; return 0; } - Students must determine the output order.
notes_text: For the initialization list question, using : vals(20), s(s_init) in the initialization list is more efficient than default-constructing then reassigning. For construction order, members are constructed in declaration order (ABC then DEF) before the XYZ constructor body runs.

images.description: Two code exercises side by side: left asking about efficient initialization of Thing class members, right asking about construction order output of XYZ with ABC and DEF members

title: Review [3] - Friend Functions and Friend Classes
summary: Review exercise on friend functions (what does the friend keyword imply for operator+?) and friend classes (can DEF access ABC's private member x?).
main_text: Friend Functions exercise: What does the highlighted friend keyword imply in the code below? class Complex with public Complex(), Complex(double r, double i), friend Complex operator+(const int&, const Complex&), and private double real, imag. The operator+ implementation accesses rhs.real and rhs.imag directly. What would break if we remove the friend keyword? Friend Classes exercise: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? class ABC with private int x and public members. class DEF with public void clear(ABC& obj) { obj.x = 0; }. If not, how can class ABC grant access to DEF? Students must determine if friend declaration is needed and where to place it.
notes_text: The friend keyword grants a non-member function access to private members of the class. Without it, operator+ could not access Complex's private real and imag members. For the friend class question, DEF cannot access ABC's private x without ABC declaring DEF as a friend.

images.description: Two code exercises: left showing Complex class with friend operator+ and asking about the friend keyword, right showing ABC and DEF classes asking about private member access

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the solutions to the review exercises from the previous slides.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Solutions section, providing answers to the review exercises on constructor identification, const correctness, initialization lists, construction order, and friend functions/classes.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review exercises before looking at the solutions.

title: Identify that Constructor - Solution
summary: Provides the solutions: s1 uses Student::Student() default constructor, s2 uses Student::Student(string, int) or Student::Student(const char*, int), vals uses vector<int>::vector<int>(int).
main_text: Prototype what constructors are being called here. Given the Student class with default constructor Student() and initializing constructor Student(const string& name), with private members string name_, int id_, vector<int> grades_. In main(): s1 (Student s1;) uses Student::Student() - the default constructor. s2 (Student s2("Tommy", 12345);) uses Student::Student(string, int) or Student::Student(const char*, int). dat (vector<int> vals(10);) uses vector<int>::vector<int>(int) - the vector constructor that takes a size argument.
notes_text: The s2 answer notes both (string, int) and (const char*, int) because the string literal "Tommy" could be implicitly converted to std::string or matched as const char*.

images.description: Code showing Student class with constructors and main() with highlighted declarations, alongside the solutions listing which constructor each call invokes

title: Review [1] Solution - Const Answers
summary: Solutions: f1 won't compile (modifying const vector), b.size() prints 3, trailing const means no data members can be modified nor non-const member functions called.
main_text: Const function arguments solution: Will this code compile? No, modification of x in f1() because x is const vector<int>&. Indicate what will be printed (assuming it compiles): b.size() will be 3 (f2 changes b to "Bye" which has 3 characters). Const member functions solution: What does the highlighted const keyword imply? No data members can be modified nor non-const member functions called. In void f1(const Item& arg): int x = arg.bar(); is fine because bar() is const. arg.foo(); causes a Compiler Error because foo() is not const and cannot be called on a const reference.
notes_text: The key insight is that a const reference can only call const member functions. This ensures the promise of not modifying the object is maintained throughout the call chain.

images.description: Same code layout as slide 51 with answers filled in: No for compilation, 3 for output, and explanation of const member function implications
labels: No, modification of x in f1()
No data members can be modified nor non-const member functions

title: Review [2] Solution - Initialization Lists and Construction Order
summary: Solutions: use : vals(20) initialization list for efficiency; construction order prints ABC, DEF, XYZ (members first in declaration order, then object).
main_text: Constructor Initialization Lists solution: The most efficient way to initialize vals to size 20 is to use the initialization list: Thing::Thing(const std::string& s_init) : vals(20) { s = s_init; }. The vals(20) in the initialization list calls vector's constructor directly with size 20, avoiding the two-step default-construct-then-resize approach. Construction Order solution: The code prints ABC, DEF, XYZ. When XYZ x1 is constructed: first ABC m1's constructor runs (prints "ABC"), then DEF m2's constructor runs (prints "DEF"), finally XYZ's constructor body runs (prints "XYZ"). Members are constructed in the order they are declared in the class, before the object's own constructor body executes.
notes_text: Note that s could also be initialized in the initialization list as : vals(20), s(s_init) for maximum efficiency. The construction order is always determined by declaration order, not initialization list order.

images.description: Same layout as slide 52 with solutions: initialization list : vals(20) shown in code, and ABC/DEF/XYZ output order shown

title: Review [3] Solution - Friend Functions and Classes
summary: Solutions: friend grants operator+ access to Complex's private members; removing it breaks rhs.real/rhs.imag access; DEF can access ABC.x only with friend declaration.
main_text: Friend Functions solution: What does the highlighted friend keyword imply? That function can access Complex private members. What would break if we remove it? Could not access rhs.real / rhs.imag because they are private members of Complex. The operator+ function needs to access temp.real, temp.imag, and rhs.real, rhs.imag directly. Friend Classes solution: Can DEF::clear() access obj.x? Yes (this implies ABC has declared DEF as a friend). If not, how can class ABC grant access to DEF? Add friend definition - specifically, class ABC would add 'friend class DEF;' inside its class body to grant DEF access to its private members.
notes_text: Friend declarations break encapsulation intentionally and should be used sparingly. They are most commonly used for operator overloading where the operator needs access to private data of the class it operates on.

images.description: Same layout as slide 53 with answers: friend grants private access, removing it breaks real/imag access, ABC must add friend class DEF declaration
labels: That function can access Complex private members

title: Not Responsible for Material Past This Point
summary: Divider slide indicating that material after this point is supplementary and not required for exams or assignments.
main_text: YOU ARE NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR MATERIAL PAST THIS POINT. This indicates that the following slides cover advanced or supplementary topics (nested types, static members) that are not required material for the current course assessments.
notes_text: While not required, the supplementary material on nested types and static members is useful for understanding more advanced C++ patterns.

title: Nested Types Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the supplementary topic of nested types (structs/classes defined inside other classes).
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Nested Types section, a supplementary topic. Nested types allow defining structs or classes inside other classes, which is useful for helper types like linked list nodes and iterators that exist solely to support the outer class.
notes_text: Nested types are common in standard library implementations (e.g., iterators) and in data structure implementations.

title: Duplicate Types - The Problem
summary: Shows how using the same struct name (Item) for both integer and double linked lists causes a duplicate type name error.
main_text: Recall linked lists use a helper struct to model each item in the list. It stores a value (of a certain type) and a pointer to the next item. If we want to use a different type list, we would need a different Item struct, but would need to name it differently. For an integer linked list: struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; used by class ListInt. For a double linked list: struct Item { double val; Item* next; }; - this causes an ERROR because of a duplicate type name. Solutions include: Different names (IntItem vs DoubleItem), Templates (more later), or Nested Types.
notes_text: This motivates the need for nested types. Without them, you would need unique names for every helper struct, which becomes unwieldy in large projects.

images.description: Code showing integer linked list Item struct and ListInt class, then a duplicate double linked list Item struct that causes an error

title: Nested Types - Definition and Usage
summary: Explains how nested types (structs/classes defined inside another class) can share names across different classes and be accessed with scope resolution.
main_text: A struct or class can be defined inside another and is known as a nested type. Good practice to nest 'helper' types (i.e. structs/classes that exist SOLELY in support of the outer class). Nested types can share the same name but have different implementations when defined inside of different objects. Examples include linked list Item structs and Iterators (later in the class). Code shows class ListInt with a nested struct Item { int val; Item* next; } and class ListDbl with a nested struct Item { double val; Item* next; }. Both use the name Item without conflict because they are scoped to their respective classes. In main(): ListInt::Item x; x.val = 3; accesses the integer version. ListDbl::Item* p; p = ld.find(2.5); accesses the double version.
notes_text: Nested types are scoped to their enclosing class, so ListInt::Item and ListDbl::Item are distinct types despite sharing the same simple name. This is a form of namespace-like scoping within classes.

images.description: Code showing ListInt and ListDbl classes each with their own nested Item struct, and main() using scoped type names ListInt::Item and ListDbl::Item

title: Declaring and Using Nested Types
summary: Explains scoping rules for nested types: non-members must scope with classname::typename, but member functions can use the type directly.
main_text: Non-members must scope the type name: classname::typename. Member function code does not have to scope the type once inside the member function scope. However, notice the return type of a function is not inside the member function scope. Code shows class ListInt with nested struct Item { int val; Item* next; }, ListInt() constructor, void append(int v), and Item* find(int v) const. In the implementation: void ListInt::append(int v) { Item* x = new Item; // no scoping needed inside member function }. But for the return type: ListInt::Item* ListInt::find(int v) const { ... } - the return type requires scoping because it appears before the function scope begins. In main(): ListInt mylist; ListInt::Item* p = mylist.find(2); // requires scoping the type.
notes_text: The scoping rule for return types is a common gotcha. C++11's trailing return type syntax (auto find(int v) const -> Item*) can avoid this issue.

images.description: Code showing ListInt class with nested Item, member function implementations demonstrating when scoping is and isn't needed

title: Static Members Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the supplementary topic of static data members and static member functions.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Static Members section, a supplementary topic. Static members are variables or functions that belong to the class itself rather than to any particular instance. The following slides cover the motivation for static members, their declaration and initialization, and practical examples like unique ID generation and the singleton pattern.
notes_text: Static members are an important concept for understanding class-level behavior versus instance-level behavior.

title: One For All - Unique ID Problem
summary: Poses the problem of assigning unique IDs to USCStudent objects as they are created, asking how this can be accomplished.
main_text: As USCStudent objects are created we want them to have unique IDs. How can we accomplish this? The class USCStudent has a constructor USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = ________; // ???? } with private string name and int id. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); and USCStudent s2("Jill"); should each have unique IDs. The question is: what value should id be assigned, and how can we ensure each new student gets a different ID?
notes_text: This motivates the need for a shared counter that persists across all instances. A regular data member would give each instance its own counter, which doesn't solve the problem.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent class with blank ID assignment in constructor and main() creating two students

title: One For All - Counter as Data Member (Wrong Approach)
summary: Shows that making a counter a regular data member doesn't work because each instance gets its own separate counter.
main_text: Can we just make a counter data member of the USCStudent class? What's wrong with this? The class USCStudent has a constructor USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = id_cntr++; } with private int id_cntr, string name, and int id. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2. The problem is that id_cntr is an instance member, meaning each USCStudent object has its own id_cntr. When s1 is created, s1.id_cntr is uninitialized. When s2 is created, s2.id_cntr is also uninitialized. The counters are not shared between objects.
notes_text: Each instance having its own counter defeats the purpose. We need a single counter shared by all instances, which is exactly what static members provide.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent with id_cntr as regular member, demonstrating the problem of separate counters per instance

title: One For All - Static Members Solution
summary: Introduces the static keyword to create a shared counter variable that belongs to the class rather than any specific instance.
main_text: It's not something that we can do from within an instance. A student doesn't assign themselves an ID, they are told their ID. Sometimes there are functions or data members that make sense to be part of a class but are shared (only 1 exists) amongst all instances. The variable or function doesn't depend on the instance of the object, but just the general class (family of objects). We can make these 'static' members which means one definition shared by all instances. The class USCStudent has USCStudent(string n) : name(n) { id = id_cntr++; } with private static int id_cntr, string name, and int id. The static member must be initialized outside the class: int USCStudent::id_cntr = 1;. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2.
notes_text: The static keyword changes the storage class of the member from per-instance to per-class. There is exactly one copy of id_cntr shared by all USCStudent objects.

images.description: Code showing USCStudent with static int id_cntr and its initialization outside the class, demonstrating shared counter

title: Static Data Members - Declaration and Initialization
summary: Details how to declare static members with the static keyword, initialize them outside the class in a .cpp file with class scope, and how they are shared.
main_text: A static data member is a single variable that all instances of the class share. Can think of it as belonging to the class and not each instance. Declare with keyword static. Initialize outside the class in a .cpp (can't be in a header). Must be scoped with class name. Code shows class USCStudent with static int id_cntr declared in the class, and int USCStudent::id_cntr = 1; initialization outside the class. In main(): USCStudent s1("Tommy"); // id = 1, USCStudent s2("Jill"); // id = 2. A diagram shows USCStudent::id_cntr as a single box with value 3 (after two increments), with s1 (Tommy, id 1) and s2 (Jill, id 2) as separate instance boxes, illustrating that id_cntr is shared while name and id are per-instance.
notes_text: Static data members must be defined (initialized) outside the class in exactly one .cpp file. Putting the initialization in a header would cause multiple definition errors across translation units.

images.description: Diagram showing USCStudent::id_cntr as single shared box with value 3, and two separate instance boxes for s1 (Tommy, 1) and s2 (Jill, 2)

title: Example: Class Constants (string::npos)
summary: Uses std::string::npos as a real-world example of a static class constant, explaining its use with find() to indicate no match.
main_text: Sometimes there are constants that are useful to define for a class but the same value for all instances. std::string::npos is such a constant. It is used as an input value for a length parameter that means 'until the end of the string'. It is returned by a call to string::find() or string::rfind() to indicate 'no match'. Code example: string s1 = "cs104"; if(s1.find("103") == string::npos) { cout << "We're not in 103 anymore" << endl; }. The find function searches for "103" in s1 and returns string::npos if not found.
notes_text: string::npos demonstrates a practical use of static const members. It is a sentinel value that all string objects share, defined once at the class level.

images.description: Code example showing string::npos usage with find() to check if a substring exists in a string

title: Example: Class Constants (string::npos) - Implementation
summary: Shows that string::npos is implemented as static const size_t npos = (size_t)-1, which is the largest unsigned value (all 1s in binary).
main_text: std::string::npos is set to the largest unsigned value supported by the system (all 1s in binary) which can be achieved by casting -1 (which is all 1s in signed binary) to an unsigned value. A simplified string class shows: class string { public: static const size_t npos; ... };. The initialization outside the class: const size_t string::npos = (size_t)-1;. Casting -1 to size_t produces the maximum unsigned value because -1 in two's complement is all 1 bits, and reinterpreting those bits as unsigned gives the maximum value.
notes_text: This is a clever use of two's complement representation. Since size_t is unsigned, casting -1 to size_t gives the maximum possible value, which serves as an ideal 'not found' sentinel.
