images.description: Code showing simplified string class with static const size_t npos declaration and its initialization to (size_t)-1

title: Another Example: Singleton Pattern
summary: Demonstrates static member functions and the singleton design pattern using a President class that allows only one instance.
main_text: In addition to static data members, static member functions are also allowed. Static member functions do NOT take a 'this' pointer (not executing on an instance). They are called by preceding with 'className::'. They can access private members of the class. Code shows class President with public static President* makePresident(string name) and void printName() const, private string name_, President(string name) : name_(name) {} (private constructor to disallow other instances), and static President* thePres. Initialization: President* President::thePres = nullptr;. The makePresident function checks if(nullptr == thePres) then creates thePres = new President(name); and returns thePres. In main(): President* p = President::makePresident("Carol"); President* p2 = President::makePresident("Mark"); p->printName(); // prints "Carol", p2->printName(); // still "Carol" because only one instance is ever created.
notes_text: The singleton pattern ensures exactly one instance of a class exists. The private constructor prevents external creation, and the static factory method controls instantiation. This is a common design pattern in C++.

images.description: Code showing President class implementing singleton pattern with private constructor, static member function makePresident, and static pointer thePres

title: A Related Example - Static Members for Shared State
summary: Shows how static members can represent shared state (all US citizens share one president) and why private static members need accessor functions.
main_text: All US Citizens share the same president, though it changes over time. Rather than wasting memory for each citizen to store a pointer to the president, we can make it static. However, private static members can't be accessed from outside functions. For this we can use a static member function. Code shows class USCitizen with USCitizen() constructor, private static President* pres, string name, and int ssn. In main(): USCitizen c1; USCitizen c2; President* curr = new President; USCitizen::pres = curr; // won't compile because pres is private. The solution is to provide a static setter function.
notes_text: This example motivates static member functions as accessors for private static data. The next slide shows the complete solution with a setPresident static function.

images.description: Code showing USCitizen class with private static President pointer that cannot be accessed directly from main()

title: Static Member Functions
summary: Explains static member functions: they operate at class level, cannot access instance data, are called with className::, and serve as accessors for static data.
main_text: Static member functions do tasks at a class level and can't access data members (since they don't belong to an instance). Call them by preceding with 'className::'. Use them to do common tasks for the class that don't require access to an instance's data members. Static functions could really just be globally scoped functions but if they are really serving a class' needs it makes sense to group them with the class. Code shows class USCitizen with public USCitizen() and static void setPresident(President* p) { pres = p; }, private static President* pres, string name, and int ssn. In main(): USCitizen c1; USCitizen c2; President* curr = new President; USCitizen::setPresident(curr); ... President* next = new President; USCitizen::setPresident(next);.
notes_text: Static member functions are essentially namespaced free functions that have access to private static members. They are called with the class name, not an instance, reinforcing that they operate at the class level.

images.description: Code showing USCitizen class with static setPresident function and main() calling it via USCitizen::setPresident()

summary: Section divider indicating older material follows, likely from a previous version of the course.
main_text: This slide contains just the word OLD, indicating that the following slide contains older or archived material that may have been part of a previous iteration of the course.

title: Review: Parts of a C++ Class
summary: Summarizes the four main parts of a C++ class: data members, constructors, member functions, and destructors, with a LListInt example.
main_text: What are the main parts of a class? Data members: What data is needed to represent the object? Constructor(s): How do you build an instance? Member functions: How does the user need to interact with the stored data? Destructor: How do you clean up after an instance? Example shows class LListInt (a linked list of integers) with public: LListInt() (default constructor), LListInt(int n) (initializing constructor), ~LListInt() (destructor), void push_front(int n), void pop_front(), void printList() const. Private: Item* get(size_t loc) helper function and Item* head pointer. This example demonstrates all four parts: head is the data member, two constructors handle creation, push_front/pop_front/printList are member functions for interaction, and ~LListInt handles cleanup of dynamically allocated nodes.
notes_text: This summary slide ties together all the major concepts from the unit. Every well-designed class should carefully consider each of these four aspects: what data it holds, how it is constructed, what operations it supports, and how it cleans up.

images.description: Code showing LListInt class with all four parts labeled: data members (head), constructors (default and initializing), member functions (push_front, pop_front, printList), and destructor (~LListInt)
